newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia's economy minister tries to woo investors.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia's economy minister tries to woo investors.

text.p: Bosnia-Herzegovina is an attractive opportunity for foreign investors but they must hurry or investments might be more expensive next year, the country's economy minister said on Wednesday.
Trying to woo foreign investment, economy minister Hasan Muratovic said the country offered both a "quick buck" and long-term investment profits despite the devastating legacy of a 3-1/2 year war.

"There is an extraordinary chance for investment in Bosnia-Herzegovina. All you have to do is compare the situation a year ago and now," Muratovic told a meeting of foreign economic experts in Sarajevo.

Bosnia emerged from a 43-month war in 1995 in desperate need of foreign aid to rebuild its infrastructure. But the government is also eager to attract direct foreign investment to boost economic growth.
Bosnia, which had a medium-developed industrial economy before the 1992-1995 war, still boasted a number of viable industries which could be revived with relatively small funding, Muratovic said.

"Look at what we import and seek your guidance there," he said. Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation statistics show a trade deficit of about $370 million created by imports of food, transport equipment, reconstruction material and textile products.
The World Bank estimates that the industrial sector operates at about 10 percent of capacity.

Muratovic urged foreign donors to offer favourable deals to companies from their countries on condition that they enter joint ventures in Bosnia with local firms. "That is also a great way of helping," he said.
But foreign experts agree the country needs to free its economy from the influence of socialist-era management and carry out a speedy privatisation if it wants to see investors flocking to Bosnia.
"Muratovic made a very strong case for investment in Bosnia and he certainly identified the good points," said Rory O'Sullivan, World Bank Sarajevo director.
"There is however another aspect which is the need for the political process to move forward and to implement rapid privatisation and restructuring of the economy," he said.

O'Sullivan agreed with concerns voiced by numerous foreign analysts who say that Bosnia's fragile peace depends on the political will of Serb, Croat and Moslem leaders to build a state as required by a 1995 peace accord.
"If the politicians would stop discussing politics and get on with economic problems of the country... At the moment there's more concern about politics and not about economics," O'Sullivan said.
"There are many tremendous opportunities now and a smart investor will look out for them, but the government has to be seen to be going ahead with reforms and privatisation."

International officials have proposed a set of economic reform laws needed for a deal with the International Monetary Fund and a fund-raising conference as well. They include a central bank law, foreign debt, budget and tariff laws.

Political bickering has so far blocked progress and a donors' conference has been postponed for the second time this year, moving it from its originally scheduled March date to April and then for an unspecified date before June this year.
Foreign investors were looking for assurances that state-owned enterprises would be privatised so that they had equal market opportunities, O'Sullivan said.
